Depiction: God the Father has no human face or body; use light, cloud, fire or radiance. The Holy Spirit is dove, wind or flame, never human.
Depiction: Treat battles, death and crucifixion seriously; avoid lingering gore.
Depiction: No sexually explicit content; non-sexual nudity may follow the text.
Depiction: Show all peoples with dignity, without ethnic or religious caricature.
Depiction: Visionary creatures follow the text, strange and fearsome rather than comic.
Era: Kingdoms, exile and return
People: Israelites and neighboring Levantine, Mesopotamian and Persian peoples.
Dress: Tunics, cloaks, court robes, priestly linen and period armor.
Buildings and objects: Villages, palaces, temples, city gates and exile settlements.
Technology: Iron and bronze tools, chariots, siege works and scrolls; no modern objects.

SELECTED CHARACTERS: Daniel (prophet of Babylon); Darius the Mede

CANON (fixed identity of the figures, places and things present; the scene plan decides pose, expression and action):
- Daniel: a lean, dignified Judean man in his youth grown to a grave, graying elder; olive-brown skin; dark hair cropped close and a short trimmed beard flecked with grey; deep-set, steady eyes and a calm, thoughtful face. Signature outfit: a long undyed linen tunic under a plain indigo wool cloak with a blue fringed hem. Props: a small leather scroll case slung at the hip.
- Darius the Mede: early sixties; broad, settled build; olive-brown skin; short grey-streaked beard and hair under a tall royal cap; lined, steady face with heavy brows. Signature outfit: a long purple court robe over a cream tunic, with a gold-embroidered collar and a deep blue sash. Signature prop: a signet ring of gold on his right hand.
- The den of lions: a deep circular stone pit cut into bare earth beside a royal enclosure, its walls of dressed grey limestone rising high above a sandy floor. A heavy wooden lid and an iron-banded gate sit at the rim, reached by a worn stone stair. Dry scrub and a few palms grow at the edge; no plants inside the pit.
- Only Daniel (prophet of Babylon), Darius the Mede, the den of lions have this canon look; other selected people get clearly different faces, hair and clothing colours.

SECTION PLACE (the same in every image of this story section; draw it as written, seen from wherever the scene plan's setting and composition place the view):
Stone-walled pit den beneath a palace, with a raised edge and a heavy stone at its opening, lit from above; a king's palace courtyard nearby

SCENE PLAN (this moment's place, time and action; obey the rules, brief, canon and style):
Primary subject: Daniel, unhurt, being drawn up from the pit by hands at the rim
Action: Attendants haul Daniel up over the raised edge while he steadies himself.
Setting: At the rim of the den where the wooden lid and iron-banded gate are open, in view from the edge, with the pit below
Secondary elements: Darius kneeling at the edge with arms extended toward Daniel; a few attendants gripping ropes; the lions crouched unharmed far below in the shadowed pit
Mood: Relief, awe and quiet joy
Time of day: Early dawn light warming to morning, clear still air
Composition: Eye-level view from the rim, Daniel centered rising out of the pit with Darius leaning in from the right

ART STYLE: Classical
Rendering: Stylized, painterly, mysterious and expansive. The painterly treatment belongs to the depicted world itself, not to a photographed physical artwork.
Negatives: Avoid photorealism or a photographic look. Avoid childish/cartoonish styling. Never present the scene as a painting on a wall, gallery piece, framed artwork, fresco, mural, poster, manuscript page, or printed illustration. Do not show canvas texture, paper edges, matting, border, mockup, or surrounding room. The depicted world must fill the image edge-to-edge.
Palette: Mature, grounded color; rich but restrained contrast.
Lighting: Luminous, dramatic lighting.
Materials and texture: Gritty, raw texture; avoid polished digital smoothness.
Composition: Cinematic, immersive viewpoint; heroic but grounded.
